Clinical Reference

Atrial Fibrillation

On this page
A supraventricular tachyarrhythmia with disorganized atrial activation and an irregularly irregular ventricular response — no organized P waves — whose two dangers are stroke (stagnant left-atrial-appendage clot) and tachycardia-mediated heart failure.
Most common sustained arrhythmia Lifetime risk ≈ 1 in 3 (age ≥55) ≈5× stroke risk Anchor: rate control + anticoagulation
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story

Normal sinus rhythm is a metronome: the sinoatrial (SA) node fires, a single wavefront sweeps the atria, both atria contract, and the AV node meters the impulse to the ventricles. Atrial fibrillation replaces that single orderly wavefront with a storm of continuously circulating micro-wavelets and rotors at rates of 400–600 per minute. The atria quiver instead of contracting.

AF needs two ingredients: a trigger and a substrate. The classic trigger is ectopic firing from muscular sleeves inside the pulmonary veins (Haïssaguerre, 1998) — this is why pulmonary-vein isolation is the anatomical target of ablation. The substrate is a remodeled, fibrotic, stretched atrium (from hypertension, valve disease, obesity, sleep apnea, aging) that can sustain re-entry once triggered. Every episode of AF further shortens atrial refractoriness and lays down fibrosis, so the arrhythmia becomes progressively easier to hold — the aphorism "AF begets AF." The earlier you restore sinus rhythm, the less remodeling has accrued — the rationale behind early rhythm control (EAST-AFNET 4).

a calm lake (sinus rhythm) whipped into chop by wind. A single trigger gust (pulmonary-vein ectopy) on an already-choppy, shallow lake (a fibrotic atrium) sets up countless little swirling eddies that keep each other going. The AV node is a narrow spillway that only lets some of that chaos through to the ventricle below — which is why the pulse is fast and irregularly irregular.

Trigger + substrate → self-sustaining AF → the three downstream harms: rapid irregular ventricular response, loss of atrial kick, and left-atrial-appendage stasis with embolism.
Diagnostic ECG: irregularly irregular R–R intervals, absent P waves, fibrillatory baseline.
CardioNetworks: [ ] · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons: Afib ecg (CardioNetworks ECGpedia).jpg
The AV node is the "gatekeeper" that meters fibrillatory impulses to the ventricle — the target of every rate-control drug.
Madhero88 · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons: Conductionsystemoftheheart.png
The whole guide hangs on four levers, each interrupting one step of the cascade: rate-control drugs slow AV-node conduction (β-blockers, non-dihydropyridine CCBs, digoxin); rhythm-control drugs & ablation suppress the triggers/substrate (antiarrhythmics, pulmonary-vein isolation); anticoagulation interrupts appendage thrombus formation (DOACs, warfarin); and upstream/risk-factor therapy (weight loss, BP, OSA, alcohol) shrinks the substrate itself.

🩺 Clinic — outpatient diagnosis, rate/rhythm strategy & stroke prevention
Assess

When to suspect & how it presents

🔍

Presentation — symptom / sign, frequency & why

AF ranges from a racing, fluttering chest to a completely silent finding on a smartwatch or a routine pulse check. Roughly one-third of patients are asymptomatic — which is exactly why an incidental irregular pulse should never be dismissed. Symptom burden can be graded with the EHRA score (I–IV): I none, IIa mild, IIb moderate (bothersome), III severe (daily activity limited), IV disabling.

Symptom / signApprox. frequencyWhy it happens
Palpitations~55–65%Rapid, irregular ventricular response felt as fluttering/pounding; beat-to-beat stroke-volume variation from irregular filling
Fatigue / reduced exercise tolerance~55–70%Loss of atrial kick + rate-related drop in cardiac output; blunted rate response to exertion
Dyspnea~40–55%Elevated LA pressure, loss of atrial contribution to LV filling, rate-related ischemia/pulmonary congestion
Asymptomatic / incidental~30–40%Adequately controlled rate; gradual onset with adaptation; found on exam/wearable/ECG
Dizziness / light-headedness~20–35%Transient low output during rapid rates or post-conversion pauses
Chest pain / pressure~15–25%Demand ischemia (rapid rate ↑ myocardial O₂ use, ↓ diastolic coronary filling)
Decompensated heart failure~15–25%Tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy or unmasking of latent LV/valve disease
Syncope / presyncope~5–10%Very rapid rates, long post-conversion pauses (tachy–brady), or WPW with rapid AV conduction
Embolic stroke / TIA as first presentation~2–5%LAA thrombus embolizes before AF is ever diagnosed — "AF discovered after stroke"

Exam: irregularly irregular pulse, variable-intensity S1, a pulse-deficit (apical rate > radial rate because weak beats don't transmit), and possible signs of the precipitant (thyroid, HF, valve murmur).

An irregularly irregular pulse is AF until proven otherwise. The two mimics are multifocal atrial tachycardia and frequent PACs/PVCs — the ECG distinguishes them in seconds.
Workup

What to order & when

🧪

Labs & imaging — with the trigger to order

12-lead ECGEvery suspected case. Diagnostic = irregularly irregular R–R, no discrete P waves, fibrillatory baseline. Also defines rate, QRS width, pre-excitation (WPW), prior MI, LVH.First
Ambulatory monitorIf paroxysmal/suspected but ECG normal: Holter (24–48 h), 2-week patch, or implantable loop recorder. Wearable/single-lead ECG ≥30 s of AF meets the 2023 diagnostic threshold. Use after cryptogenic stroke.If paroxysmal
TTE (echocardiogram)In essentially all new AF: LVEF, LA size/volume, valve disease (esp. mitral stenosis → valvular AF), wall thickness, pericardium. Guides rhythm strategy & identifies substrate.New AF
TEEBefore cardioversion when AF ≥48 h / unknown duration and patient not therapeutically anticoagulated ≥3 wks — excludes LAA thrombus so you can safely convert now.Pre-cardioversion
TSH, free T4Every new AF — hyperthyroidism is a reversible driver and changes rate-control choice.New AF
CBC, BMP (K⁺/Mg²⁺), LFTsAnemia/infection as precipitants; renal & hepatic function set DOAC and antiarrhythmic dosing; electrolytes affect QT and arrhythmia.Baseline
Coags (PT/INR, aPTT), lipids, HbA1cBaseline before anticoagulation; screen the vascular/metabolic risk factors that are also stroke-risk components.Baseline
Sleep studyScreen for OSA (highly prevalent; CPAP reduces AF recurrence). Low threshold if obese, snoring, resistant HTN, or AF recurs despite therapy.Risk factor
The workup answers three questions at once: Is it really AF? (ECG/monitor), What is driving it? (echo, TSH, sleep, labs), and What is safe to give? (renal/hepatic function, structural heart disease dictates which antiarrhythmic is allowed).

Key ECG & imaging findings — what they mean

FindingWhere / whenWhy it appears / what it changes
Irregularly irregular R–R, no P waves, fibrillatory baseline12-lead ECG (diagnostic; ≥30 s on single-lead)Chaotic atrial activation with variable AV conduction — the diagnosis
Rapid, wide, very irregular complexes (>250 bpm, "FBI")ECG at presentationPre-excited AF via accessory pathway (WPW) — changes therapy entirely (no AV-nodal blockers)
Ashman phenomenon (occasional wide beat after a long–short cycle)ECGAberrant conduction, not a PVC — a benign mimic of ectopy in AF
Reduced LVEF / global hypokinesisTTE, new AF or HFTachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy vs pre-existing HFrEF — steers β-blocker choice & rhythm control (CASTLE-AF)
Enlarged LA volume index (>34 mL/m²)TTEMarker of chronic substrate/remodeling; predicts AF recurrence & lower cardioversion success
Moderate–severe mitral stenosis / mechanical valveTTEDefines "valvular AF" → warfarin only, DOACs contraindicated
LAA thrombus or dense spontaneous echo contrast ("smoke")TEE, before cardioversionContraindicates immediate cardioversion — anticoagulate & re-image

Interpreting the labs — why each value moves

LabDirection & meaning in AFConfounders / false moves
TSH ↓ (free T4 ↑)Hyperthyroidism — a reversible driver; raises ventricular rate & embolic riskNon-thyroidal illness & amiodarone both perturb thyroid tests; check free T4
K⁺ / Mg²⁺ ↓Lowers arrhythmia threshold & prolongs QT — repletion (K⁺ >4, Mg²⁺ >2) stabilizes rhythmDiuretics, GI losses, alkalosis lower them; hemolysis falsely raises K⁺
Creatinine ↑ / CrCl ↓Directly sets DOAC & antiarrhythmic (dofetilide, sotalol) dosingMuscle mass, hydration, trimethoprim/cimetidine shift creatinine without true GFR change
BNP / NT-proBNP ↑Atrial stretch & HF burden; supports rate/volume managementAF itself raises natriuretic peptides; obesity lowers them, age/CKD raise them
Troponin ↑Demand ischemia from RVR, or true ACS as a precipitantRate-related small rises are common; trend & correlate with ECG/symptoms
Hemoglobin ↓Anemia worsens rate/symptoms & raises the bleeding-vs-anticoagulation stakesDilution vs true blood loss — identify the driver before anticoagulating
Digoxin level ↑Toxicity risk (target 0.5–0.9 ng/mL); worse with ↓K⁺, ↓Mg²⁺, renal failure, amiodarone/verapamilDraw ≥6 h post-dose; early levels read falsely high
Score

Stroke risk — CHA₂DS₂-VASc

🧮

The single most important decision in AF: who gets anticoagulated

Every AF patient needs a stroke-risk estimate. The 2023 ACC/AHA guideline anchors the anticoagulation decision on annual thromboembolic risk, estimated by CHA₂DS₂-VASc. Anticoagulate when the score is ≥2 in men or ≥3 in women (≈≥2%/yr risk); at score 1 (men) / 2 (women) it is reasonable to offer it (shared decision); at 0 (men) / 1 (women, sex point only) no anticoagulation.

CHA₂DS₂-VASc calculator

C — Congestive HF / LV dysfunction +1
H — Hypertension (or on treatment) +1
A₂ — Age ≥ 75 +2
D — Diabetes mellitus +1
S₂ — Prior Stroke / TIA / thromboembolism +2
V — Vascular disease (MI, PAD, aortic plaque) +1
A — Age 65–74 +1
Sc — Sex category female +1
0
Select the factors that apply.
Annual stroke risk by score0 ≈ 0.2%/yr · 1 ≈ 0.6% · 2 ≈ 2.2% · 3 ≈ 3.2% · 4 ≈ 4.8% · 5 ≈ 7.2% · 6 ≈ 9.7% · 7 ≈ 11.2% · 8 ≈ 10.8% · 9 ≈ 12.2% (adjusted rates, Friberg 2012 cohort — used by MDCalc). Note the female sex point only adds risk in the presence of ≥1 other risk factor.
Don't use age 65 both ways — age ≥75 scores 2 (and you do not also add the 65–74 point). The clock resets: 65–74 = 1, ≥75 = 2.
Score

Bleeding risk — HAS-BLED

🩸

Flag & fix modifiable bleeding risk — not a reason to withhold

HAS-BLED estimates 1-year major-bleeding risk. A high score (≥3) does not mean "don't anticoagulate" — it means find and fix the modifiable factors (control BP, stop NSAIDs/excess alcohol, correct labile INR) and monitor more closely.

H — Hypertension (SBP >160) +1
A — Abnormal renal function +1
A — Abnormal liver function +1
S — Stroke history +1
B — Bleeding history / predisposition +1
L — Labile INR (if on warfarin) +1
E — Elderly (age >65) +1
D — Drugs (antiplatelet/NSAID) +1
D — Alcohol ≥8 drinks/week +1
0
Select the factors that apply.
Other scores — link out (don't guess the math) For continuous/nomogram tools, use MDCalc: CHA₂DS₂-VASc · HAS-BLED · ATRIA bleeding · EHRA symptom class.
Treat

Chronic management — rate, rhythm & anticoagulation

Two parallel tracks in every AF patient: stroke prevention (CHA₂DS₂-VASc) runs independent of the rate-vs-rhythm symptom decision.
💊

Track 1 — Rate control ladder

Target rate: a lenient resting goal of <110 bpm is non-inferior to strict <80 for most patients (RACE II). Go stricter (<80 resting) if symptomatic at higher rates, if LV function is declining (tachycardia-mediated CM), or during rhythm-control preparation.

1
First-line — β-blocker OR non-DHP calcium channel blocker
Choice driven by LVEF: β-blocker (or CCB) if EF preserved; β-blocker (not CCB) if HFrEF
▾
Both slow AV-node conduction so fewer fibrillatory impulses reach the ventricle. β-blockers blunt sympathetic drive at the node; non-DHP CCBs (diltiazem/verapamil) block L-type Ca²⁺ channels in nodal tissue. Non-DHP CCBs are contraindicated in HFrEF (negative inotropy) — use a β-blocker there.
DrugStartTitration → Target / MaxWhy / notesIf intolerant / alt
Metoprolol tartrate25 mg PO BIDDouble q1–2 wk → 50–100 mg BID (max 400 mg/day)Default oral BB; short-acting for titrationSwitch to succinate once stable
Metoprolol succinate (XL)50 mg PO daily→ 100 → 200 mg daily (max 400)Once-daily; preferred if concomitant HFrEF/CADCarvedilol/bisoprolol
Carvedilol3.125 mg PO BIDDouble q2 wk → 6.25 → 12.5 → 25 mg BIDGDMT β-blocker of choice in HFrEFBisoprolol, metoprolol succ.
Bisoprolol2.5 mg PO daily→ 5 → 10 mg dailyCardioselective; HFrEF-validatedMetoprolol succinate
Atenolol25 mg PO daily→ 50–100 mg dailyRenally cleared — avoid in CKDMetoprolol (hepatic)
Diltiazem ER120 mg PO daily→ 180 → 240 → 360 mg dailyNon-DHP CCB; good if BB-intolerant & EF preservedVerapamil
Verapamil ER180 mg PO daily→ 240 → 360–480 mg/dayConstipation; ↑ digoxin levelsDiltiazem
Unknown home dose?Start at the low end of the ladder (e.g., metoprolol tartrate 25 mg BID or diltiazem ER 120 mg daily), recheck HR/BP, and titrate — do not guess a high maintenance dose. Monitor for bradycardia, hypotension, fatigue, and (β-blocker) bronchospasm on initiation.
2
Add-on — Digoxin
Add when a single agent fails, or in HFrEF/hypotension where more BB/CCB isn't tolerated
▾
Digoxin enhances vagal tone at the AV node (slows conduction) and is a mild positive inotrope — useful in HFrEF and when BP won't tolerate more β-blocker. Weak at controlling exertional rate (vagal effect is overridden by sympathetic drive), so it's an add-on, not monotherapy for active patients.
DrugLoadMaintenanceTarget / monitorCaution
Digoxin0.25 mg IV/PO q6h ×2–3 doses (≈0.75–1.5 mg/24 h)0.125–0.25 mg PO daily (0.0625–0.125 if CKD/elderly)Serum level 0.5–0.9 ng/mL; check K⁺/Mg²⁺/renalNarrow window; toxicity ↑ with hypokalemia, renal failure, amiodarone/verapamil
3
Refractory — amiodarone rate control or AV-node ablation + pacemaker
When combined agents fail or aren't tolerated
▾

Amiodarone can control rate when others fail or the patient is hypotensive (it has AV-nodal effects with less negative inotropy) — but its long-term toxicity (thyroid, lung, liver, skin, eyes) makes it a last resort for rate control. AV-node ablation + permanent pacemaker ("ablate and pace") guarantees rate control in drug-refractory, highly symptomatic patients but makes them pacemaker-dependent — reserve for the elderly/frail after shared decision-making; consider CRT if LVEF reduced.

🎵

Track 2 — Rhythm control (when & how)

Pursue rhythm control when: symptoms persist despite adequate rate control; AF with HFrEF (CASTLE-AF — ablation cut death/HF hospitalization); younger patients / first episode; AF diagnosed within ~1 year (EAST-AFNET 4 — early rhythm control reduced CV death/stroke/HF); or difficulty achieving rate control.

The antiarrhythmic (AAD) selection rule — driven by structural heart diseaseThis is the single most tested fact: the drug is chosen by what heart disease is present, because of proarrhythmia.
SubstratePreferred AAD(s)Dose ladderAvoid / why
No/minimal structural diseaseFlecainide, propafenone (Class Ic); dronedarone; sotalolFlecainide 50 mg BID → 100–150 mg BID (max 300/day) · Propafenone 150 mg TID → 300 mg TIDIc drugs contraindicated in CAD/HF (CAST — ↑ mortality)
"Pill-in-the-pocket"Flecainide or propafenone single doseFlecainide 200–300 mg once · Propafenone 450–600 mg once (always with an AV-nodal blocker on board; first dose supervised)Only if no structural disease & BP stable
Coronary artery diseaseDronedarone, sotalol, dofetilide, amiodaroneDronedarone 400 mg BID · Sotalol 80 mg BID → 120–160 mg BID (renal, QT) · Dofetilide 125–500 mcg BID by CrCl/QTNo flecainide/propafenone
Heart failure (HFrEF)Amiodarone, dofetilideAmiodarone load 400 mg BID–TID ×1 wk → 400 mg/day → 200 mg/day maintenance · Dofetilide in-hospital initiationDronedarone contraindicated in NYHA III–IV / recent decompensation (ANDROMEDA ↑ death); sotalol/Ic avoided
In-hospital initiation requiredDofetilide and sotalol must be started in-hospital with continuous ECG and CrCl-based dosing — both prolong QT and can cause torsades. Dronedarone and amiodarone can be started outpatient.
A
Cardioversion (restore sinus)
Electrical (synchronized DCCV) or pharmacologic — anticoagulation rules are mandatory
▾

Anticoagulation around cardioversion (elective): if AF ≥48 h or unknown duration → therapeutic anticoagulation ≥3 weeks before or a TEE to exclude LAA thrombus, then continue ≥4 weeks after (then indefinitely per CHA₂DS₂-VASc). AF clearly <48 h: lower risk but still anticoagulate periprocedurally and decide long-term by score.

Electrical: synchronized biphasic shock 120–200 J. Pharmacologic: ibutilide 1 mg IV over 10 min (repeat once; watch QT/torsades, pre-treat with Mg), flecainide/propafenone (no structural disease), or IV/oral amiodarone.

B
Catheter ablation — pulmonary vein isolation (PVI)
Reasonable first-line for symptomatic paroxysmal AF; superior to drugs for maintaining sinus
▾

PVI electrically isolates the pulmonary-vein triggers. Now a Class 1 option as first-line rhythm control in symptomatic paroxysmal AF (EARLY-AF, STOP-AF First — cryoablation beat AADs) and in AF + HFrEF (CASTLE-AF — mortality/HF-hospitalization benefit). CABANA: no significant reduction in the primary composite intention-to-treat, but improved AF burden, symptoms, and quality of life. Anticoagulation continues per CHA₂DS₂-VASc regardless of ablation success.

🛡️

Track 3 — Anticoagulation (DOAC dosing)

DOACs are preferred over warfarin for non-valvular AF (equal/superior stroke prevention, less intracranial bleeding — RE-LY, ROCKET-AF, ARISTOTLE, ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48). Warfarin only for mechanical valves or moderate–severe mitral stenosis.

Apixaban — a direct factor Xa inhibitor; the DOAC with the broadest tolerability across renal function.
Edgar181 · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons: Apixaban.png
AgentStandard doseDose reduction criteriaNotes / reversal
Apixaban5 mg PO BID2.5 mg BID if ≥2 of: age ≥80, weight ≤60 kg, Cr ≥1.5 mg/dLBest data in CKD; twice daily. Reversal: andexanet alfa / 4F-PCC
Rivaroxaban20 mg PO daily with dinner15 mg daily if CrCl 15–50Once daily; take with food for absorption. Reversal: andexanet / 4F-PCC
Dabigatran150 mg PO BID75 mg BID if CrCl 15–30Dyspepsia; avoid CrCl <15. Reversal: idarucizumab (specific)
Edoxaban60 mg PO daily30 mg daily if CrCl 15–50 or weight ≤60 kgAVOID if CrCl >95 (less effective). Reversal: andexanet / 4F-PCC
WarfarinTitrate to INR 2.0–3.0Genotype/interaction-dependentOnly choice for mechanical valve / mod–severe MS. Reversal: vitamin K + 4F-PCC
Cannot take long-term anticoagulation (recurrent major bleeding, falls with bleeding)? Consider percutaneous LAA occlusion (WATCHMAN) — PROTECT-AF/PREVAIL showed non-inferior stroke prevention vs warfarin in selected patients.
Monitor

Titration & follow-up cadence

📈

What to recheck, and when

  • Rate-control titration: recheck HR/BP (and symptoms) 1–2 weeks after each dose change; resting ECG to confirm rate; ambulatory monitor if exertional symptoms persist.
  • Digoxin: level + K⁺/Mg²⁺/renal 5–7 days after start or dose change and with any renal change.
  • Sotalol / dofetilide: ECG for QTc at each dose; renal function; hold/adjust if QTc >500 ms.
  • Amiodarone: baseline + q6-month TSH & LFTs; annual CXR/PFTs if symptoms; annual eye exam; skin/neuro review.
  • Anticoagulation: renal & hepatic function at least yearly (more often if CKD/elderly) to keep DOAC dose correct; warfarin INR per protocol.
  • Risk factors: BP, weight/BMI, glucose, OSA therapy adherence, alcohol — the substrate levers (LEGACY: ≥10% weight loss markedly reduces AF burden).
Prevent

Prevention, risk-factor & USPSTF

🛡️

Substrate modification & relevant screening

GradeRecommendationRelevance to AF
BScreen adults ≥18 for hypertension (office BP, confirmed out-of-office)HTN is the leading modifiable AF driver (atrial stretch/fibrosis)
BScreen adults for abnormal glucose / type 2 diabetes (age 35–70 with overweight/obesity)Diabetes is a CHA₂DS₂-VASc risk factor & AF substrate
BScreen adults for unhealthy alcohol use & provide brief counselingAlcohol dose-dependently triggers AF ("holiday heart"); reduction cuts recurrence
BOffer/refer to intensive behavioral counseling for obesity (BMI ≥30)≥10% weight loss reduces AF burden & recurrence (LEGACY)
IUSPSTF found insufficient evidence to screen asymptomatic adults for AF with ECG (2022 statement)Note: opportunistic pulse/wearable detection is still reasonable case-finding

Also: treat OSA (CPAP), encourage exercise, up-to-date vaccinations (influenza/COVID reduce cardiovascular events), and lipid/vascular risk management.

Escalate

When to refer / send to ED

🚑

Red flags — don't manage in clinic

Send to ED / admit for: hemodynamic instability (SBP <90, shock), ongoing ischemic chest pain, acute decompensated HF/pulmonary edema, syncope, uncontrollable RVR despite oral agents, new AF with a very rapid wide-complex rhythm (suspect WPW pre-excitation — do NOT give AV-nodal blockers), or a stroke/TIA presentation.

Refer to cardiology/EP: for rhythm-control candidacy, ablation, AAD initiation requiring monitoring, LAA occlusion evaluation, or when AF coexists with significant valve disease/HFrEF.

🛏️ Wards — acute inpatient rate control, cardioversion & anticoagulation bridging
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria & initial profile

  • AF with RVR not controlled by initial ED therapy, or requiring IV agents/continuous telemetry
  • New AF precipitating or worsening heart failure or demand ischemia
  • Planned cardioversion needing anticoagulation bridging or TEE
  • Initiation of an antiarrhythmic that requires monitored loading (dofetilide, sotalol)
  • AF as a symptom of another acute illness (sepsis, PE, thyroid storm, GI bleed) — admit for the driver
  • Syncope, or embolic event (stroke/TIA/limb ischemia)
Ask "why now?" — new AF is often the messenger, not the message. Screen for sepsis/infection, PE, ACS, hyperthyroidism, alcohol, electrolyte derangement, hypoxia, and post-operative state. Treating the driver often converts the rhythm.

Treat

Acute inpatient management

💊

Rate control for AF with RVR — the IV ladder

1
Stable RVR, preserved EF — IV β-blocker or diltiazem
▾
DrugBolusInfusion / repeatNotes
Diltiazem IV0.25 mg/kg (~20 mg) over 2 minMay repeat 0.35 mg/kg (~25 mg) at 15 min → infusion 5–15 mg/hFast, titratable; avoid in HFrEF/hypotension
Metoprolol IV2.5–5 mg over 2 minRepeat q5 min up to 15 mg → transition to POPreferred if ischemia/high adrenergic drive
Esmolol IV500 mcg/kg over 1 min50–200 mcg/kg/min infusionUltra-short half-life — ideal if tenuous BP (titrate off fast)
Verapamil IV2.5–5 mg over 2 minRepeat 5–10 mg at 15–30 minMore negative inotropy than diltiazem
2
HFrEF / hypotension — digoxin ± amiodarone
▾

Digoxin IV 0.25 mg q6h (max ~1.5 mg/24 h) load then 0.125–0.25 mg daily — controls rate without dropping BP; slow onset (hours). Amiodarone IV 150 mg over 10 min → 1 mg/min ×6 h → 0.5 mg/min ×18 h — helps rate control in critically ill/hypotensive patients (and may convert to sinus — anticoagulate first if AF ≥48 h, since conversion can embolize a clot).

Do NOT give AV-nodal blockers (diltiazem, verapamil, β-blockers, digoxin, adenosine) if the QRS is wide/irregular and pre-excitation (WPW) is suspected — blocking the AV node shunts conduction down the accessory pathway → VF. Use procainamide/ibutilide or cardiovert.
3
Rhythm control on the floor
▾

Elective cardioversion once anticoagulation criteria met (≥3 wks therapeutic or TEE-negative). In-hospital dofetilide/sotalol loading with QTc monitoring for maintenance. Rate-control failure or ongoing symptoms → EP consult for ablation.

Monitor

Daily management

📈

What to trend each day

  • Rate & rhythm on telemetry — resting & with activity; document conversions/pauses
  • Volume/perfusion: BP, weight, I/O, HF exam — rate control and diuresis together
  • Electrolytes daily while titrating (K⁺ >4, Mg²⁺ >2), renal function for dosing
  • QTc if on sotalol/dofetilide/amiodarone/ibutilide
  • Anticoagulation status & bleeding; the "why now?" driver's trajectory
  • Digoxin level if used, with any renal change
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Floor → ICU triggers

Transfer for: hypotension/shock needing pressors or unstable RVR requiring urgent synchronized cardioversion; RVR driving ongoing ischemia or acute pulmonary edema; need for a continuous antiarrhythmic/vasoactive drip with close hemodynamic monitoring; pre-excited AF (WPW) with instability; or the underlying driver (septic shock, massive PE, GI hemorrhage) itself needing critical care.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: resting HR consistently <110 on an oral regimen, hemodynamically stable ≥24 h, anticoagulation started/decided with teaching done, driver treated or plan in place, QT-drug loading complete if applicable, and follow-up (cardiology/EP, INR/renal labs) arranged.

Home

Rate controlled, stable, independent, reliable for meds/follow-up.

Home health

Home + nursing for INR checks / new anticoagulation / med titration teaching.

SNF

Needs 24h skilled nursing (e.g., deconditioned elder, post-stroke needs) but <3 h therapy/day.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Post-embolic-stroke deficits able to tolerate ≥3 h therapy/day, ≥2 disciplines.

LTAC

Rare — prolonged complex care (e.g., vent weaning after critical-illness AF).

Hospice / palliative

Permanent AF within advanced HF or terminal illness; comfort-focused rate control.
🫀 ICU — unstable AF, cardioversion & the critically-ill patient
Admit

ICU triggers & the unstable pathway

🚨

When AF belongs in the unit

AF with serious signs due to the rate — hypotension/shock, ischemic chest pain, acute heart failure/pulmonary edema, or altered mental status → immediate synchronized cardioversion (ACLS). Sedate if able; don't delay for anticoagulation when the patient is crashing.
Synchronized cardioversion delivers the shock on the R wave to avoid the vulnerable T-wave period.
BAC 2003 · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons: BAC 2003 Antilles PC EX3 FIG3.png
The stakes of AF: cardioembolic stroke — larger and more disabling than most other stroke subtypes.
0475ramosk · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons: 1-s2.0-S0967586810002766-gr2.jpg

Energy: synchronized biphasic 120–200 J for AF (escalate if unsuccessful); 50–100 J for atrial flutter. Confirm sync mode each attempt.

Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs, targets

  • Continuous ECG + arterial line if unstable or on vasoactive/antiarrhythmic drips (beat-to-beat BP through rate changes)
  • Central access for amiodarone infusion (phlebitis via peripheral) & vasopressors
  • Electrolytes q6–12 h while loading antiarrhythmics: keep K⁺ >4.0, Mg²⁺ >2.0 (empiric MgSO₄ 2 g IV often helps rate/conversion)
  • QTc with each antiarrhythmic dose; telemetry for torsades
  • Trend the driver: lactate/ScvO₂ in shock, troponin in ischemia, cultures in sepsis
Support

Drips — rate, rhythm & pressure

💉

Which drip, why, and the dose

AgentMechanismDoseEffectWhen to pick
Amiodarone IVMulti-channel (K⁺, Na⁺, Ca²⁺, β); AV-node slowing + rhythm conversion150 mg over 10 min → 1 mg/min ×6 h → 0.5 mg/min ×18 h (≈1 g/day)Rate control ± conversion, little hypotensionCritically ill / HFrEF / hypotensive RVR
Diltiazem IVL-type Ca²⁺ channel block at AV node0.25 mg/kg bolus → 5–15 mg/h infusion↓ Ventricular rateStable RVR, preserved EF
Esmolol IVβ1 blockade (t½ ~9 min)500 mcg/kg bolus → 50–200 mcg/kg/min↓ Rate, rapidly reversibleTenuous BP where you may need to stop fast
Digoxin IVVagal AV-node slowing + inotropy0.25 mg q6h load → 0.125–0.25 mg/day↓ Rate without ↓ BPHFrEF/hypotension add-on
Norepinephrineα1 > β10.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑ SVR/MAPShock — restore pressure so rate agents are tolerated
Ibutilide IVClass III (K⁺ block) — chemical cardioversion1 mg over 10 min, repeat ×1Restores sinusConvert recent-onset AF; pre-treat Mg, watch torsades
In septic/critically ill AF, the rhythm is usually a symptom of the illness (catecholamines, hypovolemia, hypoxia, electrolytes). Fix the driver first — resuscitate, oxygenate, replete Mg/K — before escalating rate/rhythm drugs. If pressure is the problem, restoring MAP with norepinephrine often slows the rate more than another AV-nodal agent would.
Cardioverting AF that has been present >48 h (or unknown duration) without anticoagulation or a negative TEE can dislodge an appendage clot — do it only if the patient is unstable because of the AF and can't wait.
Airway

Respiratory support

🌬️

AF with hypoxemia / cardiogenic pulmonary edema

AF itself doesn't need a ventilator — but the acute HF/pulmonary edema it precipitates often does. Escalate oxygenation to break the cycle (hypoxia → catecholamines → faster AF).

First step
NIV (BiPAP)
cardiogenic pulmonary edema — reduces preload/afterload, avoids intubation

6 mL/kg IBW

92–96%
correct hypoxia driving the arrhythmia
Induction cautionChoose hemodynamically neutral agents (etomidate/ketamine) — propofol can drop SVR and worsen rate-related hypotension.
Rescue

Advanced / refractory options

⚙️

When standard measures fail

Electrophysiology lab — catheter ablation (pulmonary-vein isolation) for refractory symptomatic AF.
Wolfgang Hunscher, Dortmund · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons: Herzkatheterlabor.jpg
LAA occlusion device (WATCHMAN-type) — mechanical stroke prevention when anticoagulation isn't possible.
MacWal02 · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons: Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion Device.jpg
  • Repeat/escalated synchronized cardioversion (max energy, anterior-posterior pads, pre-treat with ibutilide/amiodarone to raise success)
  • Magnesium infusion as adjunct for rate control/conversion in the critically ill
  • Esmolol/landiolol drip for adrenergic-driven refractory RVR in sepsis (short-acting, titratable)
  • Mechanical support (IABP/Impella/ECMO) for the underlying cardiogenic shock, not the AF per se
  • AV-node ablation + pacing for intractable rate in the right patient; WATCHMAN when long-term anticoagulation is truly contraindicated
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Downgrade when: off vasoactive/antiarrhythmic drips ≥6–12 h on a stable oral regimen, resting HR <110 sustained, hemodynamically stable with the driver improving (lactate normalizing, no ischemia), airway secure or extubated, and antiarrhythmic loading complete with QTc stable. Not yet if: still shocking recurrently, on an amiodarone/esmolol drip for rate, MAP dependent on pressors, or QTc >500 ms on a QT-prolonging drug.
Interactions

Comorbidity interactions & drugs to avoid

🔗

How common comorbidities change AF management

ComorbidityEffect on AFHow it changes management
HFrEFBidirectional worsening; tachycardia-mediated CMβ-blocker (not non-DHP CCB); consider digoxin; rhythm control/ablation favored (CASTLE-AF); AAD limited to amiodarone/dofetilide
HFpEFVery common; loss of atrial kick poorly tolerated (stiff LV)Rate control + aggressive volume/BP management; low threshold for rhythm control
CADIschemia from demand; shared risk factorsβ-blocker preferred; avoid flecainide/propafenone; dronedarone/sotalol/dofetilide/amiodarone allowed
HypertensionLeading modifiable driver (atrial stretch)BP control is substrate therapy; ACEi/ARB may reduce recurrence; counts in CHA₂DS₂-VASc + HAS-BLED
OSAStrong trigger; predicts recurrenceTreat with CPAP — improves rhythm-control & ablation success
ObesityDose-dependent AF risk & burden≥10% weight loss reduces burden/recurrence (LEGACY); structured risk-factor program
HyperthyroidismReversible cause; ↑ ventricular responseTreat thyroid; rate control harder — may need higher β-blocker; rhythm often self-corrects once euthyroid
CKD / ESRD↑ both stroke & bleeding riskDOAC dose reduction by CrCl; apixaban best-studied in advanced CKD; avoid dabigatran if CrCl <15; avoid edoxaban if CrCl >95
Prior stroke/TIA+2 on CHA₂DS₂-VASc — high recurrenceAnticoagulate (timing after acute stroke per size/hemorrhage risk, "1-3-6-12 day" rule)
WPW / pre-excitationAccessory pathway can conduct AF at lethal ratesAvoid all AV-nodal blockers; procainamide/ibutilide or cardioversion; definitive pathway ablation
Drugs to avoid / use with caution in AF: non-DHP CCBs (diltiazem/verapamil) in HFrEF; flecainide/propafenone with CAD or structural heart disease (CAST); dronedarone in NYHA III–IV/decompensated HF (ANDROMEDA) and permanent AF (PALLAS); AV-nodal blockers in pre-excited AF (WPW); DOACs with mechanical valves or moderate–severe mitral stenosis (use warfarin); sotalol/dofetilide with QTc >500 ms or significant renal impairment without adjustment; and NSAIDs (bleeding + fluid retention) in anticoagulated patients.
🧩

Special situations

Post-operative AF

New AF complicates ~20–40% of cardiac surgery and is common after major thoracic/non-cardiac surgery — driven by inflammation, catecholamines, volume shifts, and pain. Manage the precipitants, control rate (β-blocker preferred unless contraindicated), and cardiovert if unstable. It often self-terminates, but it is not benign: it raises stroke risk, so anticoagulate based on CHA₂DS₂-VASc weighed against the post-surgical bleeding window, and arrange follow-up because recurrence is common.

AF after recent PCI / ACS — "triple therapy" dilemma

A patient needing both a DOAC (for AF stroke prevention) and antiplatelets (for a stent) bleeds more the longer they overlap. Current practice minimizes triple therapy: give a short peri-PCI period of triple therapy (often just the hospital stay, up to ~1 week), then drop aspirin and continue DOAC + a P2Y₁₂ inhibitor (usually clopidogrel) for ~6–12 months, then DOAC monotherapy long-term (AUGUSTUS, PIONEER AF-PCI, RE-DUAL PCI). Favor a DOAC over warfarin and clopidogrel over ticagrelor/prasugrel for the combination.

Atrial flutter

Typical (cavotricuspid-isthmus-dependent) flutter shares AF's thromboembolic risk and the same anticoagulation rules, but is far more curable — CTI ablation has high success and low risk. Rate control is harder (organized 2:1 conduction locks at ~150 bpm); it frequently coexists with or degenerates into AF.

Anticoagulation timing after an acute ischemic stroke

Balance re-embolization against hemorrhagic transformation using infarct size — the classic "1-3-6-12 day" rule: start/restart anticoagulation about day 1 for a TIA, day 3 for a small stroke, day 6 for a moderate stroke, and day 12 for a large stroke (individualize with imaging and neurology input).

Pearls

High-yield pearls

💡

The things that change management (and get tested)

Rhythm ≠ risk. Restoring sinus rhythm does not let you stop anticoagulation — thromboembolic risk follows CHA₂DS₂-VASc, not the rhythm on today's monitor (AFFIRM).
WPW + AF can kill. In pre-excited AF (irregular, wide, >250 bpm — "fast, broad, irregular"), AV-nodal blockers (adenosine, diltiazem, verapamil, digoxin, β-blockers) funnel conduction down the accessory pathway → VF. Use procainamide/ibutilide or cardiovert.
Never give flecainide/propafenone alone. Class Ic drugs can organize AF into 1:1-conducted atrial flutter at lethal ventricular rates — always pair with an AV-nodal blocker, and never use them with CAD/structural heart disease (CAST).
Non-DHP CCBs are off-limits in HFrEF. Diltiazem/verapamil are negative inotropes — reach for a β-blocker ± digoxin instead.
Digoxin is a resting-rate drug. Its vagal mechanism is overridden by exertional sympathetic drive, so it's an add-on, not monotherapy for active patients — and it's dangerous in renal failure (target 0.5–0.9 ng/mL).
HAS-BLED optimizes, it doesn't withhold. A high score means fix the modifiable factors (BP, NSAIDs, alcohol, labile INR) and follow closely — not "don't anticoagulate."
Know the two DOAC traps: apixaban reduces to 2.5 mg BID only with ≥2 of {age ≥80, ≤60 kg, Cr ≥1.5}; edoxaban is avoided when CrCl >95 (loses efficacy vs warfarin).
Valvular = warfarin. Mechanical valve or moderate–severe mitral stenosis → warfarin only; DOACs are contraindicated (RE-ALIGN showed harm).
New AF in a sick patient is often the messenger. Hunt for sepsis, PE, ischemia, hyperthyroidism, hypoxia, and electrolyte gaps — Mg and K repletion are cheap, effective adjuncts, and the rhythm often self-corrects when the driver is treated.
Every cardioversion is thrombogenic. Even in the <48 h window, anticoagulate periprocedurally and for ≥4 weeks after; AF ≥48 h/unknown needs ≥3 weeks before or a TEE.
Risk-factor modification is disease-modifying therapy. ≥10% weight loss (LEGACY), CPAP for OSA, BP and alcohol control measurably reduce AF burden and recurrence — the "C" of AF-CARE.
Treat early. The atrium remodels with time ("AF begets AF"); early rhythm control (within ~1 year) improves outcomes (EAST-AFNET 4), and ablation is now first-line for symptomatic paroxysmal AF.
